sections.html:
Marshall County lies in northeast Alabama on the Tennessee River. Guntersville holds the courthouse seat, while Albertville has the most people. In 2020 the population was 97,612, housing totaled 41,245 units with 9.7% empty, and owners lived in 70.5% of occupied homes. The county appraises roughly 64,000 separate parcels.

Geography drives the bill. Compare a lake-view house near Guntersville with a rural house in the Sand Mountain area and the yearly costs can be far apart. Albertville, Arab, Boaz and Guntersville are the cities, and Cherokee Ridge, Douglas, Grant and Union Grove are towns. Arab, Boaz and the Joppa area partly lie in neighboring counties, and a sliver of Huntsville reaches into Marshall. Find out which county actually bills your parcel.

The total is built from state, county and school district levies, plus a city's in some places. Unincorporated communities such as Asbury, Claysville, Horton and Warrenton are mostly rural parcels. The county keeps two courthouses, one in Guntersville and one in Albertville, so call ahead to learn where your errand is handled.

One office handles both valuation and collection: the Revenue Commissioner, found on the courthouse's first floor. It values a house at what it would bring in an open sale to a willing buyer from a willing seller.

Take appraised value, apply the class percentage for assessed value, subtract exemptions, then multiply by the millage rate. One mill equals a tenth of a cent.

Property classAssessment percentage
Class I, utility30%
Class II, all other property20%
Class III, farm and owner-occupied residential10%
Class IV, motor vehicles15%

The state levies 6.5 mills and the county 13.5 mills, and school district and city levies sit on top. Because millage is not fixed, get today's figures from the office.

October 1 is the due date; December 31 is the last day before delinquency. The state schedule then runs on its own. February sends the delinquent list to probate court, March brings the court's meeting, April is advertising and May is the sale. In other words, a house can land on a sale list roughly five months after it goes delinquent.

Options are mailing the Revenue Commissioner, visiting the courthouse, or letting a mortgage escrow account pay. If a bill is outstanding, request the payoff before you list. The closer needs that number at the table.

Homestead Exemption I is for owner-occupied homes with an owner under 65, and it takes $4,000 off the state tax base and $2,000 off the county base.

Exemption II reaches owners over 65, blind owners and totally disabled owners with adjusted gross income below $12,000 a year, wiping out state tax and county tax on up to $5,000 of assessed value. A third exemption is available to owners over 65 or blind or totally disabled.

Class III land may also qualify for current use valuation, which taxes it on what it is worth to the owner and disregards development potential. Anyone inheriting a house with acreage should ask whether current use is already in place before selling.

Disputes over value start at the county Board of Equalization. To contest the board's ruling, file within 30 days after its final decision. Under Alabama Code 40-3-25 the board secretary and the circuit court clerk must be notified and a bond posted.

Prior-year taxes must be paid before they go delinquent, or the appeal may be dismissed, unless a supersedeas bond covers it. People overlook this. Keep paying the bill during an appeal, even if you intend to sell.

Before filing, call the Revenue Commissioner. Every parcel has a property record card listing land and buildings, and comparing yours with what stands on the lot can reveal errors.

The tax goes with the owner. A buyer should pay by December 31 even if the bill shows the seller, then verify that the deed was recorded at the probate office and have the property assessed under the buyer's own name.

Recording a deed triggers a state deed tax of $0.50 per $500 of value (Alabama Code 40-22-1). The deed travels with a form stating the real sale price. Two thirds of the tax goes to the state and one third to the county.

  • Before listing, get the current balance from the Revenue Commissioner.
  • Find out whether homestead or current use status sits on the parcel.
  • The title company will pay unpaid tax out of your proceeds.
  • After closing, see that the deed is recorded at the probate office.

A cash sale trims the list, since no lender waits on an appraisal or repair request, but clean title work is still required.

Collect the recorded deed, your latest tax receipt and the parcel number. Ask the Revenue Commissioner to confirm the balance, the exemption status and the land and buildings on the property record card. Errors on the card, such as a building that was torn down, are worth fixing before a buyer's title agent notices them.

For an inherited house, find out who is named on the deed and whether the estate has been opened, because that decides who can sign. If tenants live in the house, gather the lease. A buyer will ask for it early, and so will the closer.

Then request a written payoff, share it with the closer, and compare it with the tax line on the draft settlement statement. The two should match.

Allow time for the courthouse. With two locations, Guntersville and Albertville, a trip to the wrong one costs a morning. A short call to confirm the office, the hours and what to bring keeps the sale on schedule. If you live out of the area, ask whether the office can handle the request by phone or mail, and keep a written note of whatever answer you get.

Bring a photo ID and your parcel number whenever you go. If someone else is handling the sale for you, such as an executor, bring proof of that role as well.

sections.h2: Common situations for Marshall County sellers
sections.html:
Inherited houses and homes needing work are the usual cases. Renters live in 29.5% of occupied homes, so some owners are selling a rental with the tenant still there.

Heirs have a distinct problem. An estate can take a year to open, and meanwhile tax notices keep coming in the late owner's name. Missing December 31 starts interest and the probate court timetable.

Cash Home Buyers will purchase a Marshall County house in its present condition, whether it has back taxes, half-done repairs or an estate still being settled. The tax payoff is taken from proceeds by the title company.

faqs.q: How much is property tax in Marshall County?
faqs.a: That varies with assessed value, exemptions, and the city and school district. The state charges 6.5 mills and the county 13.5 mills, with school and city levies added.

faqs.q: When is Marshall County property tax due?
faqs.a: Payment is due October 1 and delinquent after December 31. You can pay at the courthouse, by mail or through mortgage escrow.

faqs.q: Who do I call about a Marshall County assessment?
faqs.a: Contact the Revenue Commissioner downstairs at the courthouse. Valuations, new-owner assessments and exemption questions all go through that office.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Marshall County house with unpaid property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. Closing normally pays the balance out of your proceeds. Get a payoff number from the Revenue Commissioner before accepting an offer.

faqs.q: What is the Alabama deed tax?
faqs.a: Alabama Code 40-22-1 sets it at $0.50 per $500 of value. The deed must come with a form stating the real purchase price.
